items.title: AI Agents Now the Enterprises Fastest Growing Exposed Attack Surface - Infosecurity Magazine
items.summary: Infosecurity Magazine Home » News » AI Agents Now the Enterprises Fastest Growing Exposed Attack Surface. The rapid adoption of enterprise AI tools is the fastest-growing source of new exposure for businesses, and it puts them at risk to additional cyber threats, a new report has warned. Published on July 22, *the Sophos AI Security 2026 Report*, warned that AI identities have become a new attack surface as AI agents and assistants are adopted in the workplace. Knowing this, cyber-attacks are targeting the trust, credentials and access permissions surrounding these systems, which has resulted in AI identities and AI agents becoming a high-value attack surface for malicious threat actors. To address the threat of cybersecurity incidents as result of compromised AI identities, the report recommended that AI agents should be treated like human users, with access restricted to just the applications and services they absolutely need to use.

items.summary: # The Month AI Governance Became Operational. **TL;DR — June 2026 was the month in which AI geopolitics became visibly operational.** The decisive shift was not a single model launch, chip shipment, or regulatory document. It was the convergence of three control surfaces: model access, infrastructure capacity, and cyber governance. It is becoming the operational layer through which model access, cloud dependency, identity, software supply chains, and sovereign AI claims are tested. The month’s strategic signal is, therefore, straightforward: **AI advantage is shifting from who can build the best model to who can control the conditions under which model capability is accessed, secured, powered, deployed, and converted into institutional capacity.**. This edition treats the reported Anthropic/Alibaba distillation allegation, the U.S. handling of Anthropic’s Fable/Mythos access, the staggered release of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6, the rise of agentic software work, AI data-center power stress, and the June cyber incident pattern as one connected story. It was whether access to model capability can be governed once the model is exposed through commercial interfaces.

items.title: Google search is indexing public Claude artifacts
items.summary:
The big picture: Claude is the latest AI chatbot to raise questions about how public AI-generated content is handled by search engines, following similar scrutiny over ChatGPT conversations.

   In June 2025, users shared conversations with Meta's AI chatbots, including text conversations, audio clips and images they'd created on a public feed, seemingly by accident. [...] Some of the shareable apps, tools and visualizations that Claude users make are appearing in Google search results.

Why it matters:Most Claude users likely don't expect that the tools they're sharing with friends, coworkers or other intended recipients could be discoverable through the world's most popular search engine. [...] Zoom in:Indexed Claude artifacts viewed by Axios on Monday included an apparent plan opposing the dissolution of a Miami city agency that oversees park management and another document about changes to a university's academic calendar.

items.title: Users’ seemingly private conversations with Anthropic’s Claude showed up in Google search results
items.summary:
Claude conversations are private by default—the only chats affected were those that users had “shared” with someone else. Claude’s share button works the way those of most competitors do: When users select it, Claude creates a snapshot of your conversation at its own web address, meant to be sent to one person or a small group with that link.

The links do not give anyone access to a user’s full account or all chats that a user has engaged in. [...] A trove of seemingly private conversations with Anthropic’s Claude chatbot turned up in public Google search results last weekend. Some of the conversations reportedly included sensitive information like cryptocurrency wallet keys and personal details such as names and addresses.

Recommended Video

The problem affected chats where users had made use of Claude’s “share” feature—which people typically use to send a record of a conversation to another person. [...] The issue surfaced over the weekend, when members of a discussion channel about Claude on the social media site Reddit found that typing a specific search phrase into Google would pull up a long list of shared Claude conversations. Claude’s Artifacts—interactive tools and mini apps people build inside Claude—also appeared in results.

items.title: Private Claude Chats Exposed in Google and Bing Search Results | WIRED
items.summary: Claude allows users to share with other people “snapshots” of chats by creating a public URL to a specific chatbot thread. The reasons some of these URLs were indexed by major search engines comes down to the basic functions of websites, search engines, and the collision of the two when generative AI gets in the mix.

items.title: How attackers hosted a fake Claude download page on the claude.ai domain - Help Net Security
items.summary:
Artifacts are a Claude.ai feature that renders certain content such as code, documents, diagrams, or full web pages in a panel beside the chat rather than as text in the conversation.

More importantly, users can publish an artifact to a public link, letting anyone view it without a Claude account. [...] In this particular case, the artifact to which potential victims were directed rendered a fully functional page that looked like a legitimate Claude download page, and the fact that it was hosted on the Claude.ai domain completed the illusion.

The only thing revealing its true nature was a short sentence displayed in the upper left corner, saying: “Content is user-generated and unverified.” However, this disclaimer is easily missed. [...] The attacker had layered several defences on top of the payloads, and Huntress researchers had to go through considerable effort (and use Claude) to analyze them and unearth the command-and-control address.

In the end, they discovered connections to previous malware delivery campaigns.
